### Third Article: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual knowledge.

Ad tertium sic proceditur. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual knowledge: because those things that are prior and better known according to nature are posterior and less known according to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior as far as we are concerned, and simple things [are later]; but universals are [simpler, therefore] known later as far as we are concerned. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the definition falls first into our knowledge, and the parts of the definition are less universal: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man"; and universals are known later as far as we are concerned. Furthermore, we arrive [at causes] through effects and [from consequences to] principles; but universals are known later as far as we are concerned.

On the contrary is what is said in the first book of the *Physics*, that one must proceed from universals to singulars.

I respond that it must be said that in the knowledge of our intellect two things must be considered. First, indeed, that intellectual knowledge in some way takes its beginning from sensitive knowledge. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the knowledge of singulars as far as we are concerned be prior to the knowledge of universals. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from <term>potentia</term> <gloss>potency/possibility</gloss> to <term>actus</term> <gloss>act/actuality</gloss>. And whatever proceeds from potency into act first arrives at an incomplete act, which is the middle between potency and act, and then a perfect act. Now, the perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science <note>original: "scia", meaning certain knowledge</note>, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; however, the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known both in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things that are more confused are first manifest and certain to us; but later we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those contained in it, is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, both the universal whole, in which the parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole can be known; for each whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being distinctly known. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing: such as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know animal in which there is "rational" or "irrational," which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, knowing "animal" occurs to our intellect before knowing "man." And the same reasoning falls if we compare any more [universal] to a less [universal], just as the sense goes out from potency into act, so does the intellect; and that order

<column-break/>

of knowledge appears in the sense. For according to the sense we judge more [common] and then less [common] is known; in a distant object we first perceive <note>original: "opzebedit", meaning apprehendit</note> it to be a body, and then we perceive it to be an animal, and further we perceive it to be a man <note>original: "bo", meaning homo</note>, and finally [a specific person like] Socrates <note>original: "sor"</note>. Or it appears and is evident in children who from the beginning first distinguish man from [non-human things]; and in the beginning children call all men "fathers" <note>original: "pres", meaning patres</note>, but later they determine each one, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*. It is manifest that whoever knows something indistinctly still knows it in potency, whether he knows the definition or the principle, and thus he knows the <term>genus</term> <gloss>general class</gloss> and is able to know the <term>differentias</term> <gloss>specific differences</gloss>. And thus, in itself, indistinct knowledge is the middle between potency and act. And because the knowledge of singulars is prior as far as we are concerned, and the knowledge of the universal [is the object of] sensitive knowledge and intellectual knowledge. If both the sense and the intellect [perceive], the knowledge of the more [universal] is prior to the knowledge of the less and the common.

To the first, it must be said that it can be considered in a double way. In one way, through the intention of truth; and when the intention of truth and the truth itself have a relationship to many things, the abstraction of the intellect arrives at this end in such a way that it is truly posterior. As it is said in the first book *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, the universal animal either is nothing or is posterior. But Plato <note>original: "plus tonem"</note> placed universals as substances <note>original: "suba", meaning substantias</note>; and in this consideration it is true, because particulars are nothing except through participation in more universally subsisting things which are called <term>ideae</term> <gloss>Ideas</gloss>. In another way it can be considered according to the nature itself of "animality" or "humanity" as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One according to the way of generation and time, since in that way things that are imperfect and in potency are prior; and in this way the more [universal] is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal, for an animal is generated before a man <note>original: "bo"</note>, as is said in the book *On the Generation of Animals* <note>original: "de generatione animalium"</note>. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect [is prior] to that which is imperfect; and in this way the less [universal] is prior in nature, as man is to animal. For the intention of nature does not stop in the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a man.

To the second, it must be said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, because the more universal contains in itself not only "man" but also "horse"; so that the less universal contains in the future not only the more universal but also others, as man [contains] not only animal but "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our knowledge to "man." If "man" were prior in our knowledge to "animal," it would be through its reasoning [definition].

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing [is known]. In another way, when it is a part of this whole, as [with] stones [in a house], it is necessary that we first know the whole and then the parts. For we first know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defining [parts] considered absolutely are prior to us and the defined. Otherwise the defined would not be made known through them. But more [universal things] are like parts [of the definition].

<summary>This page discusses the order of intellectual knowledge, arguing that humans naturally move from universal and confused knowledge to specific and distinct knowledge. Aquinas uses the example of children calling all men "father" before they can distinguish their own parent to illustrate this progression from potency to act.</summary>
